title: Who turned the Venus de Milo into a masterpiece?
subject: art
description: Found by chance in 1820 on a Greek island, a mutilated statue entered the Louvre the following year. How did one ancient sculpture among many become the ideal of female beauty?
author: dusan-nikolic

hero.hook: One ancient statue among so many, mutilated and hard to date: it took nineteenth-century France to turn it into a myth.

blocks.text: Since its discovery, the Venus de Milo has stood, in Western eyes, for ancient beauty itself. Unearthed on the Greek island of Milos, in the Aegean Sea, it quickly passed into the hands of the French king [[Louis XVIII]]. The king handed the statue to the Louvre, which officially received it in **1821**.

The statue was visibly damaged, but it was precisely its incomplete state that drew the scholars. Reconstructing it became a **matter of national importance** in nineteenth-century France, which turned an ordinary ancient statue into a unique work of ancient Greece. Slightly larger than life, it still stands in the Louvre and draws **millions of visitors** every year.
To the Greeks, the goddess was Aphrodite. Venus is the name the Romans gave her when they adopted Greek mythology.

On April 8, **1820**, on the island of Milos, a Greek peasant partly unearthed the statue of the goddess. A French naval officer with a passion for archaeology, [[Olivier Voutier]], was sent to the site of the accidental dig. Once the statue was fully uncovered, he made a drawing of it to record the event.

blocks.caption: An academic study after a bust of the Venus de Milo, anonymous drawing (1855-1875, Musea Brugge).

blocks.text: The statue is made of **two blocks**, the upper and the lower body, joined together afterwards. It stood in a semicircular niche, flanked by two [[herms]], rectangular pillars topped with a bust. The ancient gymnasium that housed it was lost to the plow. Two inscriptions, since lost, allow it to be dated cautiously to between **150 and 50** BC. The conditions of the dig and what followed left many more questions unanswered.

sections.title: In search of the lost arms

blocks.text: The most striking feature of the statue is its **missing arms**. As soon as it arrived in France, scholars tried to reconstruct its original state. They had two other fragments found at the same site: a left hand holding an apple and a right upper arm. To contemporaries, these pieces partly filled in the missing limbs.

blocks.caption: Hypotheses for restoring the arms of the Venus de Milo: beside Mars, holding a wreath, leaning on a pillar.

blocks.text: A Venus holding an apple would recall her victory in the [[Judgment of Paris]], the episode alluded to in Homer's *Iliad* in which a Trojan prince names her the most beautiful of the goddesses. Other versions circulated: Venus standing beside the god Mars, Venus resting her arm on a column, Venus holding a laurel wreath. None prevailed, because nineteenth-century France wanted its own version of the [[Parthenon marbles]], the sculptures from the great temple of Athens kept in London.
In Greek, the name of the island, Milos, translates as "apple." A neat coincidence for a statue whose recovered hand holds that very fruit.

sections.title: A statue that became an affair of state

blocks.text: The discovery of the Venus de Milo set off a complex chain of events. Their political and cultural consequences turned an ordinary ancient statue into an icon of classical heritage. The island was then under Ottoman rule, yet it was the French who bought the statue from the peasant. Acquiring the Venus was a **political matter**.

blocks.caption: Crowds of visitors around the Venus de Milo at the Louvre today.

blocks.text: In the 19th century, ancient Greece was seen as the cradle of European civilization, and the countries of Western Europe saw themselves as **heirs of classical Greece**. French scholars compared the Venus with the works of [[Phidias]], the sculptor of the Parthenon, and tried to link her to him. In **1893**, the German archaeologist [[Adolf Furtwängler]] refuted that claim at length, on archaeological grounds. His conclusions still partly hold, but the myth of the Venus de Milo, the ideal of classical female beauty, lives on.

Historical accuracy played little part in shaping the image of the Venus de Milo. The political needs of nineteenth-century France won out over genuine attempts at research. A statue like so many others of its time became the equal of the Parthenon marbles. More than **two centuries** later, its story still echoes in every visitor to the Louvre.

events.title: The discovery
events.detail: On April 8, a peasant on Milos unearths the statue and Olivier Voutier draws it.

events.title: Into the Louvre
events.detail: Louis XVIII gives the statue to the museum, which officially receives it.

events.title: The rebuttal
events.detail: Adolf Furtwängler dismantles the link with Phidias defended by French scholars.

blocks.text: That is also why the statue has never undergone any invasive restoration. It stands **practically unchanged** since the day it was dug up. Modern scholarship offers few certainties about it. Stories fill the void, shaped by the needs of the time and the eye of the beholder.
The Venus de Milo owes its status as a masterpiece less to what is known about it than to nineteenth-century France's need for a Greek treasure of its own, and its mystery is still its strength.

sources.text: P. Jockey, The Venus de Milo: Genesis of a Modern Myth, p. 219, 225-227, 229-233.
